# No AC/Ventilation out of nowhere

When a Peugeot 208 1.2 Puretech suddenly loses all airflow through the vents after sitting parked, it feels like a system failure rather than a gradual degradation. The fact that the climate control interface remains responsiveâexcept for the lack of physical air outputâand that the rear defroster still functions electrically isolates the problem significantly. Since the vehicle has not undergone any repairs or modifications, and the accessory drive belt appears physically intact, we can rule out a catastrophic belt snap or a complete electrical short at the main control unit.

The most common cause for this specific symptom, particularly when no maintenance was performed prior to the issue, is a seized compressor clutch or an internal failure within the compressor itself. In many automatic AC systems, including those found in the 208, the compressor is driven by a belt but controlled by an electromagnetic clutch. If this clutch fails to engage due to lack of lubrication, overheating from prolonged inactivity, or age-related wear on the coil springs, the system will produce zero airflow regardless of how many degrees you set the thermostat to.

Before handing the car over to a mechanic, there are specific mechanical and electrical checks worth performing to confirm the diagnosis without disassembling the entire HVAC unit. First, inspect the compressor pulley. With the engine running and the AC switched off, observe if the pulley spins freely. If the pulley is seized or moves with excessive play, the internal bearings have failed. Next, engage the AC manually (ensure the fan is on max) and listen closely to the front of the engine bay near the compressor. You should hear a distinct "click" followed by a low hum when the clutch engages. If you hear the click but no hum, the clutch coil may be burnt out or mechanically stuck open.

Another potential culprit, often overlooked in favor of mechanical failures, is the pressure sensors within the AC system. Modern ECUs monitor high and low-side pressures via sensors to protect the compressor from damage. If a sensor fails or the system detects an abnormal pressure differential (often due to a leak), the ECU may disable the compressor clutch entirely as a safety measure. This results in zero airflow while keeping the rest of the interface functional. You can check for diagnostic trouble codes using an OBDII scanner specifically tuned for HVAC systems, though this requires specialized equipment or software that goes beyond standard error code readers.

There is also the possibility of a blown fuse or a tripped relay specific to the AC compressor circuit. While less likely given the "out of nowhere" nature without prior warning lights, it is a quick check. Locate the fuse box under the hood or in the cabin, consult the diagram on the cover, and verify the integrity of the AC compressor fuse. If the fuse is intact but the relay clicks upon activation, swap the relay with an identical one from another circuit (like the horn) to see if the issue persists.

Finally, consider the expansion valve or receiver-drier. If these components are clogged with debris or moisture, they can restrict refrigerant flow enough that the system pressure drops below the threshold required for the compressor to cycle on. However, this usually presents as weak airflow rather than a complete stop unless the blockage is total. Given the age of the car and the sudden onset, a seized clutch or a failed pressure sensor remains the highest probability. If these checks yield nothing, the system likely requires professional recharging and component replacement, as there is no DIY method to repair internal compressor bearings or replace high-pressure sensors without proper tools.
